<div class="hero">
<div class="kicker">Global energy burden atlas</div>
<h1>The 67-fold mismatch between who pays and who caused it</h1>
<p class="subtitle">
Household energy burden — the fraction families pay for energy — has never
been comparably measured across most of the world. We built the first
open-code, open-data pipeline that estimates it for 129 countries and
17,000 grid cells covering 8.2&nbsp;billion people. What we found
quantifies a moral claim policymakers have accepted for three decades but
never seen sharpened into a single number.
</p>
</div>

<div style="text-align:center;">
<div class="big-number">
  <span class="n">67×</span>
  <span class="l">per-capita cumulative CO<sub>2</sub><br/>disparity at the extremes</span>
</div>
<div class="big-number gold">
  <span class="n">129</span>
  <span class="l">countries with<br/>cell-level microdata</span>
</div>
<div class="big-number green">
  <span class="n">8.2<span style="font-size:0.6em;">bn</span></span>
  <span class="l">people covered<br/>by the atlas</span>
</div>
<div class="big-number">
  <span class="n">0.13%</span>
  <span class="l">of cumulative CO<sub>2</sub><br/>from 20 least-electrified countries</span>
</div>
</div>

## What we found

The 20 countries with the lowest household electricity access — South
Sudan, Chad, Burundi, Central African Republic, DR Congo, Burkina Faso,
Haiti, and 13 others — hold **498 million people (6.1% of humanity)** and
are jointly responsible for **0.13% of cumulative global CO~2~ emissions
since 1750**.

The 20 countries with the largest historical CO~2~ emissions — led by the
United States, China, Russia, Germany, United Kingdom, and Japan — hold
**4.8 billion people (58.5% of humanity)** and are responsible for
**82% of cumulative CO~2~**.

<blockquote>
On a per-capita cumulative basis, the average resident of the top-20
historical emitters has emitted <b>67 times more</b> cumulative CO<sub>2</sub>
than the average resident of the 20 least-electrified countries.
</blockquote>

The disparity narrows to 5-fold when the comparison uses current household
energy burden instead of household electricity access. Both framings sit
on the same moral geometry, but the 67× number is the crispest.

## Why this wasn't visible before

Prior work has measured either half of this ratio, not both. The Global
Carbon Project has published cumulative-emissions data since 2006 but
paired it with country totals rather than household burdens. The IEA
World Energy Outlook models future access-to-energy trajectories but
focuses on infrastructure gaps rather than expenditure share. The World
Bank Global Consumption Database (2010, updated 2020) provides
household-level expenditure but only for ~90 countries and only in
country-average form, missing the within-country geography where energy
poverty concentrates.

Two methodological breakthroughs made the present quantification
possible.

<div class="card-grid">
<div class="card">
<div class="kicker">Method 1</div>
<h3>Spatial synthesis at global scale</h3>
<p>A five-phase pipeline in <a href="https://github.com/ericscheier/emburdensynth"><code>emburdensynth</code></a> that combines WorldPop rasters, GADM boundaries, and the World Bank Global Consumption Database with simulated-annealing spatial allocation. Extends the U.S. DOE LEAD tool from single-country to global scope.</p>
<p><a href="methods.html">Read the methods →</a></p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<div class="kicker">Method 2</div>
<h3>Correct Net Energy Return math</h3>
<p>Naive weighted-mean-of-ratios aggregation over-estimates household energy burden by a median <b>5.7%</b> and by up to <b>1,400%</b> for hyperinflation cases like Venezuela. <a href="https://github.com/ericscheier/emburden"><code>emburden::neb_func</code></a> implements the mathematically proper NEB = 1/(1 + weighted-mean-Nh) formulation.</p>
<p><a href="methods.html#aggregation">See the divergence chart →</a></p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout">
<div class="callout-title">Caveats worth naming</div>
<p>Cumulative CO<sub>2</sub> is territorial-only; consumption-based accounting would attribute a fraction of large emerging-economy emissions to consuming countries via trade, tightening rather than loosening the reported disparity. The direction of the mismatch is robust to methodological choices. The 67-fold magnitude is a lower bound.</p>
</div>
